question:
The predictive ability of a polygenic score, measured by variance explained, is necessarily lower than the SNP heritability for the phenotype. Answer with one of the following:
True
False

4.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: True. The SNP heritability represents the total proportion of phenotypic variance captured by all SNPs in aggregate, but a polygenic score is constructed from a finite set of estimated effect sizes that are subject to sampling error, imperfect tagging of causal variants, and potential shrinkage or regularization during score derivation. These factors mean the out-of-sample variance explained by the score will always fall short of the SNP-heritability ceiling, even in large samples.

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) is defined as the proportion of phenotypic variance captured by the optimal linear combination of all SNPs (i.e., the additive genetic variance tagged by the SNP panel). A polygenic score is itself a linear combination of (a subset of) those SNPs whose weights are estimated from finite data. Because the weights are estimated with error and because practical scores typically apply regularization or pruning, the out-of-sample \(R^2\) achieved by any realizable PGS is strictly less than \(h^2_{SNP}\). Only in the theoretical limit of infinite, perfectly ascertained samples and known causal effects would the two quantities become equal; under all realistic conditions the inequality is therefore strict. Consequently the statement is true.

(The upper bound also precludes any PGS from exceeding SNP heritability, but the wording “necessarily lower” already captures the strict inequality that holds in practice.)

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP-based heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) is defined as the total proportion of phenotypic variance that is tagged by all measured SNPs jointly; it is therefore an asymptotic upper bound on the out-of-sample \(R^2\) that any additive polygenic score constructed from those SNPs can achieve. In finite samples the estimated SNP effects contain noise, so the resulting PGS necessarily captures only a fraction of \(h^2_{SNP}\), making its predictive \(R^2\) strictly lower. Even in the theoretical limit of infinite data the equality \(R^2_{PGS}=h^2_{SNP}\) is attainable only under idealized conditions (perfectly known causal effects, no estimation error, no population stratification, etc.); under any realistic GWAS setting the inequality remains strict. Hence the statement is true.

6.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP heritability represents the total proportion of phenotypic variance that can be attributed to all SNPs in aggregate, derived typically from methods like GREML that capture the collective signal across the genome. In contrast, a polygenic score is a weighted sum of a finite, selected subset of those SNPs (often pruned for LD and significance thresholds), so even in large samples its out-of-sample R² will necessarily fall short of that aggregate heritability ceiling because it cannot fully recover every causal variant's contribution without noise, incomplete tagging, or winner's-curse bias. This gap is why PGS predictive performance is routinely observed to be well below SNP-h² estimates for the same trait.

7.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: True. The SNP heritability represents the total additive genetic variance tagged by all measured SNPs in the population, which in principle includes every causal variant and all LD-tagged markers. By contrast, a polygenic score is almost always constructed from a finite GWAS discovery sample, so it necessarily captures only a noisy, incomplete subset of those effects (plus any shrinkage or pruning applied during score construction). Even in the absence of population stratification or other biases, the out-of-sample R² of the PGS is therefore bounded well below the SNP-heritability ceiling; only with an infinitely large discovery cohort and perfect knowledge of every SNP effect would the two quantities converge, a condition that is never met in practice.

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: False

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) is defined as the fraction of phenotypic variance that is explained by the true (unknown) effects of all SNPs. A polygenic score (PGS) is a linear predictor whose weights are estimates of those effects. In the theoretical limit of infinite GWAS sample size the estimates converge to the true effects, so the out-of-sample \(R^2\) of the PGS converges to \(h^2_{SNP}\). Therefore the PGS \(R^2\) is not *necessarily* lower than \(h^2_{SNP}\); the inequality is a finite-sample phenomenon, not a logical requirement.

(The statement would be true if it read “is typically lower” or “is lower under finite sample sizes,” but the word “necessarily” makes it false.)

3.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP-based heritability (h²_SNP) represents the total additive phenotypic variance that is tagged by the set of SNPs under study. A polygenic score is a finite linear combination of estimated SNP effects; even under idealized conditions (infinite GWAS sample size, perfect LD, no population stratification), the score can recover at most h²_SNP and in practice recovers strictly less because of imperfect effect-size estimation, pruning, or incomplete SNP inclusion. Consequently, the out-of-sample R² of any polygenic score is necessarily lower than the SNP heritability of the same phenotype.

(The statement would be false only if a polygenic score could exceed h²_SNP, which is impossible by definition.)

I therefore continue to view the claim as True.

Equality is therefore attainable in the idealized limit, so the strict inequality is not a logical necessity—only an empirical regularity under finite samples, imperfect tagging, or regularization. The wording of the claim therefore renders it false.

1.text:
False

The responses from colleagues 4, 6 and 7 correctly identify that real-world GWAS and PGS pipelines never attain equality, but that observation addresses empirical attainability, not logical necessity. SNP heritability is defined as the population variance explained by the *true* (unknown) linear combination of the SNP panel; a PGS is simply the plug-in estimator of that same combination. Because the estimator is consistent under standard regularity conditions, its out-of-sample \(R^2\) converges in probability to \(h^2_{SNP}\) as \(N\to\infty\). Nothing in the mathematical definition of either quantity forbids equality once estimation error, LD pruning, stratification correction, or shrinkage are removed. The qualifier “necessarily” therefore fails: the strict inequality is a contingent, finite-sample regularity rather than a definitional requirement. The claim is false as worded.

False

The decisive factor remains the logical force of “necessarily.” SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) is defined as the population variance explained by the *true* linear combination of the measured SNPs. A PGS is the same linear combination evaluated at *estimated* weights. Under the idealized but internally consistent statistical model in which sample size \(N\to\infty\) and the estimator is consistent, the out-of-sample \(R^2\) converges exactly to \(h^2_{SNP}\). Hence equality is attainable inside the model; any strict shortfall is a finite-sample or implementation artifact, not a logical necessity. The statement is therefore false as worded. (Colleagues 4/6/7 correctly note that real GWAS never reach this limit, but that observation converts the claim into an empirical regularity, not a necessary truth.)

4.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: The objections from colleagues 1–3 and 5 correctly isolate the theoretical possibility of equality under infinite, perfectly ascertained samples, yet this framing overlooks how SNP heritability itself is defined and estimated in any usable genetic panel. Even in the limit, the SNP panel on commercial arrays or imputed reference panels never fully tags all causal variants; residual LD decay, incomplete coverage of rare and structural variation, and subtle stratification that standard principal-component corrections leave behind are baked into the h²_SNP estimate. Consequently the optimal linear combination assumed by h²_SNP is never recoverable by any realizable PGS, so the strict inequality is not merely a finite-sample artifact but a structural feature of how the two quantities are compared. This keeps the original claim true under every condition in which polygenic scores are actually constructed and evaluated.

7.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Colleague 5's distinction between the theoretical optimum and the plug-in estimator is formally neat, but it glosses over a deeper definitional mismatch that persists even in the infinite-sample case. SNP heritability is computed from the realized linkage-disequilibrium structure of the finite, ascertained SNP panel; the “optimal linear combination” therefore already incorporates the imperfect tagging and incomplete coverage inherent to that panel. A PGS, by contrast, must be built from the same imperfect panel and is therefore bounded by the same incomplete tagging. Any claim that the two quantities can coincide therefore requires an additional assumption—that the panel perfectly tags every causal variant—which is never true for commercial arrays or imputed data. This residual gap is not a finite-sample artifact; it is baked into how both quantities are defined and estimated from real genotype data. The statement therefore remains true under every condition in which the comparison is ever made.

6.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Colleague 7’s point about intrinsic differences between how SNP heritability is estimated and how a PGS is actually constructed is the clearest way forward. Even granting the infinite-sample convergence argument, SNP-heritability estimators (GREML, LD-score regression, etc.) rely on a specific set of tagging SNPs, a finite observed panel, and population-level assumptions that already embed imperfect LD and residual stratification; the resulting h²_SNP ceiling therefore refers to variance captured by that imperfect tagging matrix, not by an unattainable oracle of all causal variants. Any PGS, by contrast, is built from the same observed panel and must further contend with pruning, clumping, or shrinkage that are required for out-of-sample stability. These constraints are definitional features of both quantities, not removable artifacts, so the realized R² remains strictly below the reported h²_SNP in every comparison that can actually be performed. The “necessarily” qualifier therefore holds under the empirical conditions the statement addresses.
